title: Taifa of Saltés and Huelva
capsule: The Taifa of Saltés and Huelva was a small Muslim principality on the Atlantic coast of al-Andalus, centered on the island of Saltés at the mouth of the Odiel and Tinto rivers, that emerged after the collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba around 1012–1013. It was ruled throughout its existence by a single Bakrid dynasty lord, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ʿIzz al-Dawla, who governed the estuarine territory for roughly four decades. Around 1051–1053 the taifa was forcibly absorbed by the expanding Abbadid kingdom of Seville under ʿAbbad II al-Muʿtadid. Its brief existence reflects the fragmentation (fitna) of Andalusian political authority during the first taifa period.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The territorial extent of this small coastal taifa is poorly documented; its core on Saltés island is secure, but inland boundaries are unattested in surviving sources.
